# Objects {#sec-objects} *This chapter introduces the notion of an object, one of the most central aspects of Python. Once you catch your breath, you will love that all Python values are objects.* ## Methods In Python, a value like an integer or string not only holds data. It is also packaged with a lot of useful functionality relevant to the particular type of value. When a value is packaged with such relevant functionality and meta information, programmers call it an object—and in Python, all values are objects. The associated functionality comes in the form of *methods*. You can think of methods as functions that are packaged together with the value. For example, string values have a method called `capitalize`. Try it out: ::: {#cell-1 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} x = "banana".capitalize() print(x) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Banana ``` ::: ::: To call the method on the string value, you connect the string value and the method call with a dot. So, to call a method on a value, you do the following: 1. Write the value (or a variable name that substitutes for a value). 2. Then write a `.`. 3. Then write the name of the method (like `capitalize`). 4. Then, write two parentheses to call the method. If the method takes any arguments other than the value it belongs to, then you write those additional values between the parentheses with commas in between, just as when you call a function. You can see that the method call looks just like a function call, and in many ways, calling a method works much like calling a function. The difference is that when we call a function, we say: "*Hey function, capitalize this string!*". When we call a method, we say: "*Hey string, capitalize yourself!*" So why do we need methods? Why do we need them when we have functions? It is very handy to have some relevant and ready-to-use functionality packaged together with the data it works on. You will start to appreciate that sooner than you think. Methods are almost always used with variables. So remember to make any substitutions and reductions required. When we put a method call after a *variable* like below, the variable is first substituted for its value, and *then* the method is called on the value. Consider the second line of this example: ::: {#cell-3 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} x = "banana" print(x.capitalize()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Banana ``` ::: ::: Here, `x` is first substituted by `"banana"` and *then* the method is called on that value, like this: `"banana".capitalize()`. Now write and run these examples: ::: {#cell-5 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} message = "Methods Are Cool" print(message) shout = message.upper() print(shout) whisper = message.lower() print(whisper) new_message = message.replace("Cool", "Fantastic") print(new_message) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Methods Are Cool METHODS ARE COOL methods are cool Methods Are Fantastic ``` ::: ::: You can see what these methods do. For example: `upper` returns an uppercased copy of the string. #### Exercise {#sec-first_format_exe} Write and run the following code. What do you think it does? ::: {#cell-7 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code} line = '\n\tSome text\n' print(">{}<".format(line)) line = line.strip() print(">{}<".format(line)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` > Some text < >Some text< ``` ::: ::: Make sure you do the substitution and reduction steps in your head. Be especially careful about the third line of code. Also, what do you think the special `\t` character is? #### Exercise The string methods you have tried so far have all returned a new string. Try this example: ::: {#cell-9 .cell execution_count=5} ``` {.python .cell-code} 'ATGACGCGGA'.startswith('ATG') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=5} ``` True ``` ::: ::: and this ::: {#cell-11 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code} 'ATGACGCGGA'.endswith('ATG') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=6} ``` False ``` ::: ::: What do the methods do, and what do they return? ## Using the Python documentation Now that you are well underway to becoming a programmer, you should know your way around the [Python documentation](https://docs.python.org/3). Especially the part called the [Python standard library](https://docs.python.org/3/library). There is a *lot* of details in there that we do not cover in this course. These are mainly tools and techniques for writing more efficient, extensible, robust, and flexible code. The parts we cover in this course are the minimal set that will allow you to write a program that can do *anything*. #### Exercise There is a string method that returns a secret agent: ::: {#cell-13 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code} print('7'.zfill(3)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 007 ``` ::: ::: You can look it up in the [Python documentation](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#str.zfill). #### Exercise Browse through all the [string methods](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#string-methods) to get an impression of all the functionality that is packaged with string objects. ## String formatting You have already tried string formatting in @sec-first_format_exe. String formatting is a simple but powerful technique that lets you generate pretty strings from pre-computed values. You may have noticed that many decimals are shown every time we print a floating-point number. It is not very pretty if you are only interested in two decimals. You use the `format` method (surprise) to format a string. In its most straightforward use, `format` replaces occurrences of `{}` with the arguments that are passed to it - like this: ::: {#cell-15 .cell execution_count=8} ``` {.python .cell-code} taxon = "genus:{}, species:{}".format('Homo', 'sapiens') ``` ::: #### Exercise What happens if you try this? ::: {#cell-17 .cell execution_count=9} ``` {.python .cell-code} question = "Was {} {} Swedish?".format('Carl', 'Linneaus') ``` ::: and this? ::: {#cell-19 .cell execution_count=10} ``` {.python .cell-code} question = "Was {} Swedish?".format('Carl', 'Linneaus') ``` ::: and this? ::: {#cell-21 .cell execution_count=11} ``` {.python .cell-code} question = "Was {} {} Swedish?".format('Carl Linneaus') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html} 
---------------------------------------------------------------------------
IndexError                                Traceback (most recent call last)
Cell In[11], line 1
----> 1 question = "Was {} {} Swedish?".format('Carl Linneaus')

IndexError: Replacement index 1 out of range for positional args tuple
``` ::: ::: ::: In the two last examples, the number of `{}` did not match the number of arguments to `format`. What happens when there are too few and when there are too many? #### Exercise Consider this code: ::: {#cell-23 .cell execution_count=12} ``` {.python .cell-code} s = "{} is larger than {}".format(4, 3) print(s) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 4 is larger than 3 ``` ::: ::: What will happen if you run this code? Write the code and see for yourself once you think you know. If you were wrong, make sure you understand why. #### Exercise Consider this code: ::: {#cell-25 .cell execution_count=13} ``` {.python .cell-code} language = 'Python' invention = 'sliced bread' s = '{} is the best thing since {}'.format(language, invention) print(s) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Python is the best thing since sliced bread ``` ::: ::: What will happen if you run this code? Write the code and see for yourself once you think you know. If you were wrong, make sure you understand why. #### Exercise Consider this code: ::: {#cell-27 .cell execution_count=14} ``` {.python .cell-code} my_template = '{} is the best thing since {}' language = 'Python' print(my_template.format(language, 'sliced bread')) print(my_template.format(language, 1900 + 89)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Python is the best thing since sliced bread Python is the best thing since 1989 ``` ::: ::: What will happen if you run this code? Do the substitution and reduction steps in your head. #### Exercise Think back to @sec-chocolatebars, where you calculated how many cookies you could buy for 30 kr. The bars are 7 kr. So your program looked something like this: ::: {#cell-29 .cell execution_count=15} ``` {.python .cell-code} nr_bars = 30 / 7 print('I can buy', nr_bars, 'chocolate bars!') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` I can buy 4.285714285714286 chocolate bars! ``` ::: ::: and it ran like this: `python chocolate.py` ``` I can buy 4.285714285714286 chocolate bars! ``` String formatting lets you rewrite the program like this: ::: {#cell-31 .cell execution_count=16} ``` {.python .cell-code} nr_bars = 30 / 7 message = "I can buy {} chocolate bars!".format(nr_bars) print(message) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` I can buy 4.285714285714286 chocolate bars! ``` ::: ::: Try to replace `{}` with `{:.2f}`. `format` reads the stuff after the colon in each set of curly brackets and uses it as directions for formatting the value it inserts. Try it out and see what happens if you change the number `2` to `3`, `4`, `5` or `10`. #### Exercise See if you can find the documentation for the `format` function in the [Python documentation](https://docs.python.org/3). It can do wondrous things, for this course we will only try to control the number of digits and padding with spaces. Look at the examples below. Maybe you can figure out how it works. ::: {#cell-33 .cell execution_count=17} ``` {.python .cell-code} pi = 3.14159265359 print("*{}*".format(pi)) print("*{:.3f}*".format(pi)) print("*{:.6f}*".format(pi)) print("*{:>5.3f}*".format(pi)) print("*{:>10.3f}*".format(pi)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` *3.14159265359* *3.142* *3.141593* *3.142* * 3.142* ``` ::: ::: #### Exercise {#sec-add_method} This is bonus info rather than an actual exercise. How do you think Python can figure out that adding strings is supposed to work differently than adding numbers? Remember that `'1' + '2'` is `'12'` not `3`. The answer is that all values you can add with the `+` operator have a secret method called `__add__` that defines how adding works for that type of value: ::: {#cell-35 .cell execution_count=18} ``` {.python .cell-code} s1 = "11" s2 = "22" n1 = 11 n2 = 22 print(s1 + s2) print(s1.__add__(s2)) print(n1 + n2) print(n1.__add__(n2)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 1122 1122 33 33 ``` ::: ::: This is one of many examples of how objects allow Python to implement functionality that fits each value type. This was to show how Python does this. Like yellow and black stripes in nature means "don't touch me!" -- double underscores (`__`) is Python's way of saying "do not use this!". You are supposed to use the `+` operator, not the `__add__` method. ## Indexing and slicing strings Another feature of string objects is that they allow you to extract individual parts of the string. Each character in a string is identified by its *index* in the string. To access a character in a list, you write brackets after the string. Between those brackets, you specify the index of the character you want. The first character has an index of 0; the second has an index of 1, and so on. ::: {#cell-37 .cell execution_count=19} ``` {.python .cell-code} codon = 'ATG' print("first base is", codon[0]) print("second base is", codon[1]) print("third base is", codon[2]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` first base is A second base is T third base is G ``` ::: ::: You may wonder why the index of the first character is zero and not one. That is simply the convention in programming and is so for good reason. Over time you will begin to find this useful rather than annoying. You should think of the index as the offset from the start of the string. That also means that the index is not the length of the string but the length minus one: ::: {#cell-39 .cell execution_count=20} ``` {.python .cell-code} amino_acids = 'ARNDCQEGHILKMFPSTWYV' last_index = len(amino_acids)-1 print("Last amino acid is", amino_acids[last_index]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Last amino acid is V ``` ::: ::: If you want a sub-string from a larger string (we call that a *slice*), you specify a start index and an end index separated by a colon: ::: {#cell-41 .cell execution_count=21} ``` {.python .cell-code} print(amino_acids[1:4]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` RND ``` ::: ::: When you run that, you can see that `amino_acids[1:4]` is substituted for `'RND'`, so the slicing operation produces a sub-string of `amino_acids`. You may wonder why the value at index 4 is not in the resulting sub-string. That is another programming convention: intervals are *ends exclusive*. So when you specify an interval with a start index of 1 and an end index of 4, it represents all the characters starting from 1 and up to, *but not including*, 4. So, the slice `1:4` corresponds to the characters at indexes 1, 2, and 3. The reason programmers handle intervals in this way is that it makes it easier to write clear and simple code as you will see in the exercises. #### Exercise What does this expression reduce to? ::: {#cell-43 .cell execution_count=22} ``` {.python .cell-code} "Futterwacken"[7] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=22} ``` 'a' ``` ::: ::: #### Exercise What is printed here? Do all the substitution and reduction steps and compare to the exercise above. ::: {#cell-45 .cell execution_count=23} ``` {.python .cell-code} s = "Futterwacken" print(s[7]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` a ``` ::: ::: #### Exercise What is printed here? Do all the substitution and reduction steps -- and do it *twice*. Next week you will be happy you did. ::: {#cell-47 .cell execution_count=24} ``` {.python .cell-code} dna = 'TGAC' i = 0 print(dna[i]) i = 1 print(dna[i]) i = 2 print(dna[i]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` T G A ``` ::: ::: #### Exercise {#sec-immutable_strings} What do you think happens here? Make up your mind and try out the code below: ::: {#cell-49 .cell execution_count=25} ``` {.python .cell-code} s = "Futterwacken" s[6] = 'W' ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-error} ::: {.ansi-escaped-output} ```{=html}

TypeError: 'str' object does not support item assignment
``` ::: ::: ::: Did you see that coming? Strings are *immutable*, which means that you cannot change them once you have made them. Try to figure out how to do that with the [`replace`](https://docs.python.org/3/library/stdtypes.html#string-methods) method of strings. #### Exercise When you do not specify a slice's start and/or end, Python will assume sensible defaults for the start and end indexes. ``` ::: ::: ::: Read and make sure you understand the error message. You can try to Google the error message. #### Exercise Do you think you also get an error when you specify a slice where the end is too high? Try it out: ::: {#cell-55 .cell execution_count=28} ``` {.python .cell-code} alphabet = 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvxyz' print(alphabet[13:99]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` nopqrstuvxyz ``` ::: ::: and this: ::: {#cell-57 .cell execution_count=29} ``` {.python .cell-code} alphabet = 'abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvxyz' print(alphabet[10000:10007]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ``` ::: ::: I guess that is worth remembering. #### Exercise Which character in a string named `alphabet` does this expression reduce to? ::: {#cell-59 .cell execution_count=30} ``` {.python .cell-code} alphabet[len(alphabet)-1] ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=30} ``` 'z' ``` ::: ::: #### Exercise Because intervals are "ends exclusive" ,we can compute the length of a slice as `end - start`: ::: {#cell-61 .cell execution_count=31} ``` {.python .cell-code} dna = "ATGAGGTCAAG" start = 1 end = 4 print("{} has length {}".format(dna[start:end], end-start)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` TGA has length 3 ``` ::: ::: Figure out what this code would look like if ends were included in intervals. #### Exercise Another advantage of "ends exclusive" intervals is that you only need one index to split a string in two: ::: {#cell-63 .cell execution_count=32} ``` {.python .cell-code} s = 'Banana' idx = 3 beginning = s[:idx] end = s[idx:] print(beginning + end) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Banana ``` ::: ::: Figure out what indexes you would need to use to split a sequence in two if ends were included in intervals. #### Exercise Did you look up the details of how slicing works in @sec-slicing_docs? Then you should be able to explain what happens here: ::: {#cell-65 .cell execution_count=33} ``` {.python .cell-code} s = 'zyxvutsrqponmlkjihgfedcba' print(s[::-1]) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvxyz ``` ::: ::: ## General exercises #### Exercise Will this print `Bananas rule!`? Do all the substitutions and reductions. ::: {#cell-67 .cell execution_count=34} ``` {.python .cell-code} if 'na' * 2 == "Banana"[2:]: print("Bananas rule!") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Bananas rule! ``` ::: ::: #### Exercise Will this print `Bananas rule!`? Do all the substitutions and reductions. ::: {#cell-69 .cell execution_count=35} ``` {.python .cell-code} if "{}s".format('Banana'[1:].capitalize()) == 'Ananas': print("Bananas rule!") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` Bananas rule! ``` ::: ::: #### Exercise Write a function called `even_string` that takes a string argument and returns `True` if the length of the string is an even number and `False` otherwise. E.g. `even_string('Pear')` should return `True` and `even_string('Apple')` should return `False` (remember the `modulo` operator?). #### Exercise Look at the code below and decide what is printed at the end. Then, write the code and test your prediction. If you are wrong, figure out why by revisiting the chapter about functions. ::: {#cell-71 .cell execution_count=36} ``` {.python .cell-code} def enigma(x): if x == 4: return x result = enigma(5) print(result) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` None ``` ::: ::: #### Exercise Inspect the code below and determine why it does not print that you are a super star. Test the function using various inputs and identify the mistake. ::: {#cell-73 .cell execution_count=37} ``` {.python .cell-code} def even_number(x): if x % 2: return False if even_number(4): print('You are a super star!') ``` :::
